mcqs.question: What is the correct way to set timeouts across a multi-hop call chain?
options: Set every hop's timeout to the same fixed value for consistency
Let each service pick its own timeout independently based on its own historical latency
Allocate a total budget at the entry point matching the end-to-end SLA, then divide it down the chain so each hop gets strictly less time than its caller
Set the deepest hop's timeout first, then work backward to size the outer layers
mcqs.explanation: Starting from a total, end-to-end budget and shrinking it hop by hop ensures the sum across the chain never exceeds what was promised at the top. Identical timeouts at every layer compound rather than cap total latency, purely independent per-service timeouts ignore the shared budget entirely, and sizing from the deepest hop outward doesn't guarantee the top-level SLA is respected.

mcqs.question: A gateway, a service, and a DB call are each independently set to a 5-second timeout. What's the worst-case total wait the gateway's caller could see?
options: 5 seconds, since all three timeouts are identical
Up to 15 seconds, since a slow DB call can cause each of the three 5-second waits to stack on top of each other
10 seconds, since only two of the three layers can time out simultaneously
Exactly 1.67 seconds, since the 5-second budget is automatically split evenly across the three layers
mcqs.explanation: Independent identical timeouts compound: the gateway can wait its full 5s while the service inside it waits its own full 5s while the DB call inside that waits its own full 5s, summing toward 15s in the worst case. There's no automatic even split, and nothing limits how many layers can time out together in this uncoordinated setup.

mcqs.question: What does propagating an explicit shrinking deadline through the call chain require to actually work?
options: Every service in the chain must be written in the same programming language
Every service in the chain must cooperate and respect the incoming deadline — one uncooperative hop breaks the whole scheme
The call chain must have exactly two hops, no more and no fewer
All services must share the same database
mcqs.explanation: The scheme only works end to end if every hop actually reads and respects the propagated deadline; a single hop that ignores it and uses its own fixed timeout undermines the whole design. Language choice, chain depth, and shared databases are unrelated to whether deadline propagation functions correctly.

mcqs.question: How do you enforce that every service in a call chain actually respects its allotted timeout slice, rather than just hoping it was configured correctly?
options: Trust each team's local configuration and audit it manually once a year
Pass the remaining deadline explicitly in the request, so each hop can check how much time is actually left before starting work
Add a global timeout at the load balancer only, and skip timeouts everywhere else
Require every service to use exactly the same timeout value, hardcoded
mcqs.explanation: Passing the remaining deadline explicitly lets each service check for itself whether it has time to even attempt the work, rather than relying on every team's local config being correct. Manual annual audits are far too infrequent to catch drift, a single load-balancer timeout doesn't help internal hops budget correctly, and a hardcoded uniform value reintroduces the compounding problem this design is meant to avoid.
